correctness.rationale: Digit decomposition proves every admissible number has base-B digits less than b, giving the exact local necessity. For any permitted prefix, choose unbounded s coprime to B and congruent to r modulo m1; repunit coin changes represent a corrective residue R modulo lcm(s,m1) using O_B(log(s m1)) digits. Distinct congruence-controlled exponent classes then give s_B(n)=s_b(n)=s, n≡0 (mod s) and n≡r (mod m). Greedy coin bound follows from U_(j+1)=B U_j+1. Exact enumeration over 5278 allowed parameter/residue cells confirms all modular and digit conditions in tested ranges, including direct materialization where moderate; no numerical limit is used as a proof.

The new sufficiency uses an explicit bounded-length repunit-coin adjustment preserving a prescribed low digit block. Exact priority remains subject to independent bibliographic review.

value.rationale: The fixed-base, arbitrary-modulus question is a natural missing case of the recent two-base Niven theorem. The answer is a complete sharp local-global criterion, not a routine single example: every allowed base-smooth prefix class supports infinitely many simultaneous equal-digit-sum Niven integers, while every forbidden class is absolutely empty even before imposing divisibility. The exponential power-modulus spectrum has exact size b^v out of b^(kv), with arbitrarily large digit sums and a constructive noncoprime sufficiency mechanism. This resolves a structural obstruction that cannot be read off the known coprime-modulus result.
